periods.analysis: At 57.4%, 3rd-grade reading proficiency is in yellow: safely above the 55.0% floor, but still a long walk from the 65% target. This is the first quarter in this sequence, so I am treating 57.4% as the working baseline rather than a verdict on our children, our teachers, or our families. The early item I am watching is uneven foundational-skills recovery at the school level, especially in the Grade 2-to-3 cohort at Harborview Elementary, North Pier, and Bayfront Academy where attendance and phonics-screening gaps tend to move together. The encouraging sign is that we have enough performance room to manage this deliberately if we keep the work close to classrooms and not trapped in a spreadsheet.
periods.recommendations: Launch a 10-week Harborview Reads sprint in the 12 elementary schools with the largest Grade 3 unfinished-learning rosters, using small-group phonics blocks four days per week. Pair the reading sprint with attendance outreach for students missing 10% or more of school days, with Family Success liaisons assigned by homeroom rather than by building. By the next quarter, require principals to review DIBELS and unit-assessment data every other Friday and identify students moving into or out of intensive support.

periods.analysis: The rate moved from 57.4% to 56%, a decline of -1.4 percentage points, and we remain yellow. I am concerned by the dip, but not surprised: Q4 caught the first heavy absenteeism wave after the fall respiratory season, and several schools reported interrupted small-group rotations because substitutes were covering core classrooms. The watch-item is chronic absenteeism among 3rd graders receiving Tier 2 reading support; when those students miss the intervention block, the citywide number feels it quickly. We are still above the 55.0% red line, but 56% tells me we cannot confuse activity with progress.
periods.recommendations: Protect the 30-minute intervention block at every elementary site by assigning floating substitute coverage first to Grade 3 literacy classrooms at the seven highest-absence schools. Have the Harborview Public Library deploy mobile checkout carts on the Blue Line and Dockside routes so students leave before winter break with decodable readers matched to their instructional level. Publish a weekly attendance-and-reading exception list for principals, showing students who missed two or more intervention sessions in a week.

periods.analysis: We regained ground in 2025-Q1, moving from 56% to 57.3%, a +1.3 percentage-point improvement, while still holding in yellow. That rebound matters because it suggests the protected intervention blocks and family outreach are beginning to take hold, particularly at South Harbor, Mariner, and Eastgate where coaches reported more consistent small-group minutes. I would not over-celebrate 57.3%, because the 65% target is still distant and the quarter’s gains are not yet broad enough across all campuses. The watch-item now is whether midyear movers and English learner newcomers at airport-corridor schools are being assessed and placed into reading groups within five school days.
periods.recommendations: Extend the protected intervention model through spring, but add a five-day placement standard for newly enrolled Grade 3 students at Jetport, Cedar Quay, and Bayview. Use two district literacy coaches to audit small-group rosters against assessment data so students are not sitting in the wrong level for weeks. Continue the attendance exception list, and add a family text prompt the evening before each intervention day for students with two or more prior absences.

periods.analysis: The measure improved again, from 57.3% to 58%, a +0.7 percentage-point increase, which is the strongest point in this eight-quarter run so far but still yellow. I read 58% as evidence of traction, not completion: we are making disciplined progress, yet we remain 7 percentage points below the 65% target. Spring tutoring through the Harborview Reads Saturday labs appears to have helped the students who attended six or more sessions, especially on multisyllabic decoding and fluency passages. The watch-item is summer slide, because a yellow reading measure can give back gains quickly when students lose daily practice and school-based attendance routines pause.
periods.recommendations: Convert the Saturday labs into a six-week Summer Reading Bridge at library branches in Old Port, Westview, and North Pier, with transportation vouchers for families on Routes 4, 9, and 17. Pre-enroll every rising 4th grader who scored just below proficient, and send each family a plain-language reading plan before the last day of school. Hold the 58% line by requiring summer providers to track weekly attendance and oral-reading-fluency growth, not just program enrollment.

periods.analysis: The rate fell from 58% to 56.8%, a -1.2 percentage-point movement, keeping us in yellow and reminding us that spring gains did not fully survive the summer-to-fall transition. I am concerned but not discouraged; the drop is real, and the operational explanation is also real: Summer Reading Bridge attendance was strong in Old Port but thinner in Westview and North Pier, particularly during the two July heat weeks. The first month of school also showed roster churn at Jetport and Dockside, which delayed intervention placement for some students. The watch-item is speed to service in September, because a student who waits three weeks for the right reading group has already lost the quarter’s margin.
periods.recommendations: Set a September 10 deadline for every Grade 3 student to have a current reading level, intervention assignment, and attendance-risk flag in the student information system. Reassign two literacy coaches from general professional development to direct roster-cleanup work at Jetport, Dockside, North Pier, and Westview until placement is complete. Keep Summer Reading Bridge, but redesign next year’s schedule with evening and weekend blocks so heat, family work schedules, and transportation do not quietly select students out.

periods.analysis: We moved from 56.8% to 56.6%, a slight -0.2 percentage-point decline, and the status remains yellow. The small dip is not the same as a slide, but it tells me the system is idling below where Harborview needs it to be. Classroom walk-throughs showed better fidelity to phonics routines, while attendance files still showed too many students missing on Mondays and the day after holidays, which interrupts cumulative skill practice. The watch-item is not whether we have a reading strategy; we do, but whether we are executing it with enough intensity for the students who are one benchmark band from proficiency.
periods.recommendations: Create a Monday Reading Start protocol at all elementary schools: first-period fluency practice, same-day absence calls, and make-up intervention blocks by Wednesday. Direct principals to identify the “one-band-away” cohort by name and assign each student a staff reading champion before winter break. Ask the city’s Youth Opportunity Office to coordinate with after-school vendors so homework clubs at Seaport Center and Civic Hall include 20 minutes of structured decodable reading, not just general homework help.

periods.analysis: The measure edged up from 56.6% to 56.9%, a +0.3 percentage-point gain, which keeps us yellow and shows stabilization after two softer quarters. I appreciate stabilization, but I do not mistake 56.9% for success when the target is 65%. The Monday Reading Start protocol appears to have reduced missed make-up sessions at several sites, and the one-band-away lists gave teachers a sharper target for conferences and tutoring. The watch-item is scale: the practices are working in pockets, but the citywide number will not move enough until those pockets become the normal way Harborview teaches early literacy.
periods.recommendations: Scale the Monday Reading Start protocol from pilot implementation to all 24 elementary campuses, with a common checklist reviewed by assistant principals each Friday. Fund a spring micro-grant pool for teachers serving the one-band-away cohort, limited to evidence-based materials, take-home decodable sets, and family reading nights. Add a monthly public dashboard cut by attendance-risk group so we can see whether reading gains are reaching students with chronic absenteeism, not just students already attending regularly.

periods.analysis: We improved from 56.9% to 57.9%, a +1 percentage-point gain, returning close to the prior high while remaining yellow. This is the best movement since 2025-Q1, and it suggests the citywide spread of Monday Reading Start, tighter roster management, and targeted tutoring are beginning to compound. Still, 57.9% is not 65%, and the honest story is steady recovery rather than breakthrough. The watch-item for the next cycle is persistence through summer and into September, because our pattern has shown that Harborview can gain during the school year and then lose momentum during transitions.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the practices that produced the +1 percentage-point gain by making Monday Reading Start and five-day intervention placement permanent operating expectations for 2026-27. Expand Summer Reading Bridge with guaranteed seats for every one-band-away rising 4th grader, and contract transportation support before July rather than after enrollment opens. Before the next Q3 review, require each school to submit a transition roster showing reading level, attendance risk, assigned summer contact, and first-week intervention plan for every current Grade 3 student below proficiency.

periods.analysis: Third-grade reading proficiency rose from 57.9% to 58.4%, but remains 6.6 percentage points below the 65% target. The improvement is encouraging; the school-year transition remains a risk for students below proficiency.
periods.recommendations: Keep the intervention block and reading-coach coverage in place, and use the delayed FAST review to verify which students need a revised plan.
